# Corpus Brief — Joseph A. Adler, *The Yijing: A Guide* (Oxford University Press, 2022; "Guides to Sacred Texts" series)

**Scope note.** Adler's is a modern scholarly guide, not a translation. It is the single best source in the corpus for (a) the formal rules of line position/correspondence, (b) the complete yarrow-stalk divination algorithm and Zhu Xi's reading rules, (c) the full Ten Wings strata map, and (d) the Han–Song diagram/numerology systems (Jing Fang's Eight Palaces, Shao Yong's Fuxi binary sequence, Hetu/Luoshu). Chapters: 1 What Is the Yijing? (1–28); 2 Layers of Change (29–58); 3 Yijing Divination (59–74); 4 Early History of Interpretation (75–94); 5 Early Modern Views (95–135); 6 Modern China and the West (136–154); 7 Why the Yijing? (155–162). Page numbers below are printed pages. Chinese glosses and quoted translations are Adler's own.

---

## 1. SMALLEST FRAGMENTS (the "letters")

### 1.1 The line — solid/broken, firm/yielding, young/mature
- Two line types: solid ⚊ = yang 陽 ("light, warm, rising, expanding"), broken ⚋ = yin 陰 ("dark, cold, sinking, condensing") — "although yang and yin do not appear to be what the lines originally meant" (p. 3). "solid lines are considered odd and broken ones even; solid lines are also called 'firm' (gang 剛) and broken ones 'yielding' (rou 柔)" (pp. 29–30).
- "Yin and yang are not things or substances, they are modes. Yin is the dense, dark, sinking, wet, condensing, passive, receptive, 'earthy' mode of qi; yang denotes the light, bright, rising, dry, expanding, active, creative, 'heavenly' mode." (pp. 21–22)
- **Four line types** by two binary attributes: young yang (7), mature yang (9), young yin (8), mature yin (6). "Each line is interpreted as either changing ('mature') or unchanging ('young'). Thus there are four types of lines." (p. 30) Mature lines "have reached the maximum point of their yin or yang development and are about to change their direction of development" (p. 30) — the peaks/troughs of the yin-yang sine curve (Figure 1.1).
- Possible numeric origin: Shang/Zhou markings "resemble early forms of the numbers 1 (一), 5, 6, 7, and 8, and they usually occur in groups of six... One strong possibility is that the broken line of the hexagrams evolved from the even numbers 6... and 8. The number 1, of course, is identical with the solid hexagram line." (pp. 29–30)

### 1.2 The six line-places (yaowei 爻位)
- "The six lines of a hexagram are built and numbered from the bottom up, and the complete hexagram is read as a dynamic situation developing from the bottom up. In the text, line 1 is called 'the beginning' and line 6 is called 'the top.'" (p. 30)
- Line-text naming convention: yin lines are addressed as "6", yang lines as "9" — "e.g. '6 in the fourth [position]'" (p. 35).
- **Centrality (zhong 中)**: "A line is 'central' if it is the second line of a trigram, that is, positions 2 or 5 of the component trigrams, or positions 3 or 4 of the 'nuclear' trigrams." (p. 40)
- **Correctness (zheng 正)**: "A line is 'correct' if it is a yang line in an odd-numbered position (1, 3, 5) or a yin line in an even-numbered position (2, 4, 6) — since... odd numbers are yang and even numbers are yin. Thus a yang line in the fifth position is both central and correct, as is a yin line in the second position." (p. 40)
- **Ruler of the hexagram**: "either the line that most clearly embodies the meaning of the hexagram or the line in the fifth position, the center of the upper trigram." (p. 40) — [uncertain: Adler does not enumerate ruling-line types beyond this.]
- Hexagram 63 (Jiji, Already Complete) ䷾ "is a highly auspicious hexagram because all six of its lines are correct, and lines two and five are both central and corresponding." (p. 40)

### 1.3 The trigram (gua 卦) and its attribute set
- Table 1.2 (p. 10) — the eight trigrams with chief images (xiang 象) and virtues (de 德):

| Trigram | Chinese | Figure | Image | Virtue/quality |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qian | 乾 | ☰ | Heaven | Creative |
| Kun | 坤 | ☷ | Earth | Complying |
| Zhen | 震 | ☳ | Thunder | Arousing |
| Sun (Xun) | 巽 | ☴ | Wind/Wood | Penetrating |
| Kan | 坎 | ☵ | Water | Danger |
| Li | 離 | ☲ | Fire | Clinging |
| Gen | 艮 | ☶ | Mountain | Stable |
| Dui | 兌 | ☱ | Lake | Pleasing |

Footnote (p. 10): Kan is "deep, dark water, like an abyss"; Dui is "shallower water, like a lake... with the more positive feeling of well-watered land."
- "Each trigram has a name, one or more 'images' (xiang 象), and one or more 'virtues' (de 德)." (p. 9)
- Shuogua 7 (virtues, p. 55): "Qian is strong; Kun is compliant. Zhen is active; Sun is entering. Kan is sinking; Li is clinging. Gen is stopping; Dui is pleasing."
- Shuogua 8 (animals, p. 55): "Qian is the horse; Kun is the ox. Zhen is the dragon; Sun is the fowl. Kan is the pig; Li is the pheasant. Gen is the dog; Dui is the sheep."
- Shuogua 9 (body, p. 56): "Qian is the head; Kun is the abdomen. Zhen is the foot; Sun is the thigh. Kan is the ear; Li is the eye. Gen is the hand; Dui is the mouth."
- Shuogua 10 (family, p. 56): "Qian is Heaven; therefore it is designated the father. Kun is the Earth; therefore it is designated the mother. Zhen is the first bonding yielding a male... eldest son. Sun... eldest daughter. Kan... middle son. Li... middle daughter. Gen... youngest son. Dui... youngest daughter."
- Trigram polarity definition (p. 81): "a yin trigram has a single yin line and two yang lines, except for Kun, which is all yin. A yang trigram has a single yang and two yin lines, except for Qian, which is all yang." — i.e. polarity is determined by the *minority/unique* line.

### 1.4 Nuclear / interlocking trigrams (hugua 互卦 / huti 互體)
- "another way of dividing a hexagram is into 'nuclear' or 'interlocking' trigrams... which are lines 2, 3, 4 and 3, 4, 5. For example, the component trigrams of hexagram 32 ䷟ (Heng) are Sun ☴ and Zhen ☳; the nuclear trigrams are Qian ☰ and Dui ☱. Thus up to four trigrams can potentially be used in the analysis of a hexagram." (p. 10) Attributed to Jing Fang (pp. 81–82): "This expands the interpretive possibilities by doubling the number of trigrams in terms of which to discuss and analyze a hexagram."

### 1.5 The hexagram
- 2^6 = 64; "Each hexagram is conceived to represent a pattern or type of situation, based on its particular configuration of yin and yang." (p. 3) Lower trigram = "inner", upper = "outer"; "the lower and upper trigrams roughly reflect social hierarchy, for example the relationship between minister and ruler." (p. 9)
- In Zhu Xi's divination usage the lower/inner = zhen 貞 (the question/present situation), the upper/outer = hui 悔 (the prognostication) (p. 70).
- "Pure hexagrams" (chun gua 純卦): the 8 doubled trigrams (hex. 1, 2, 29, 30, 51, 52, 57, 58), heads of Jing Fang's Eight Palaces (p. 81).
- Hexagram names are "tags": "the Mawangdui text of the Yi has different names for about half of the hexagrams... some modern scholars... have used the word 'tags' instead of hexagram 'names,' to stress their arbitrary character." (p. 30)

### 1.6 The numbers 6, 7, 8, 9 — the old/new yin/yang operators
"Two principles then apply: (1) 6 and 8 are yin lines because even numbers are yin; 7 and 9 are yang because they are odd numbers... (2) 6 and 9 are mature; 7 and 8 are young. This is because both divination methods produce these numbers as sums of 2 and 3... 6=2+2+2; 7=2+2+3; 8=2+3+3; 9=3+3+3. Thus 6 and 9 are mature because they are composed of three yin (even) or yang (odd) numbers; they are 'pure' yin or yang. 7 and 8 are young because they are mixtures of yin and yang." (pp. 30–31) Changing lines marked with a small "x" (p. 31).
- Alternate stalk-count method: final pile = 24, 28, 32, or 36; "Dividing this number by 4 yields the same 6, 7, 8, or 9" (p. 71).
- Supernumerary lines: "Hexagrams 1 and 2 each have one extra line statement, which since the Song dynasty has been interpreted to indicate all six lines changing... preceded by the expressions 'Using 9' (yong jiu 用九) and 'Using 6' (yong liu 用六)" (p. 36).

### 1.7 Sequence structures
- **King Wen (received) sequence pairs**: "each contiguous pair, after the first two, are inversions of each other — for example, Zhun (hexagram 3 ䷂) and Meng (hexagram 4 ䷃). The first two, Qian ䷀ and Kun ䷁, are opposites in terms of yin and yang lines." (p. 11) [Adler does not spell out the standard refinement that pairs where inversion is impossible (1-2, 27-28, 29-30, 61-62) use full complement — noteworthy gap; his "opposites" note on 1-2 points that way.]
- **Mawangdui sequence**: "completely different... based on the trigrams, while the received text displays no awareness of trigrams" (p. 11); trigrams "are not mentioned even once in the basic text of the Zhouyi" (p. 10).
- **Fuxi/xiantian 先天 (Prior to Heaven) sequence** (Shao Yong): "One divides into two, two divides into four, and four divides into eight." (p. 99) Binary numbering: "if we assign the value 0 to a solid (yang) line and 1 to a broken (yin) line, although the values... must be calculated from the top down, contrary to the regular way of reading a gua." Table 5.1 (p. 102): Qian ☰=0, Dui ☱=1, Li ☲=2, Zhen ☳=3, Sun ☴=4, Kan ☵=5, Gen ☶=6, Kun ☷=7. Circular 64-hexagram diagram: "Qian, with a value of 0, is at the top and the numbers proceed down the left side to Fu (value 32) at the bottom; it then resumes at the top with Gou (33) and moves down the right side to Kun (64)." (p. 103)
- **King Wen/houtian 後天 (After Heaven) sequence of trigrams** (Shuogua 5.1, Table 2.1, p. 52): Zhen ☳ east → Sun ☴ southeast → Li ☲ south → Kun ☷ southwest → Dui ☱ west → Qian ☰ northwest → Kan ☵ north → Gen ☶ northeast. "When plotted in a circle this sequence describes a clockwise circulation. Traditional Chinese cartographic convention places south at the top." (p. 52)
- **Family (xiang) sequence** (Shuogua 7–10, Table 2.2, p. 53): Qian father, Kun mother, Zhen eldest son, Sun eldest daughter, Kan middle son, Li middle daughter, Gen youngest son, Dui youngest daughter. "This sequence... would not describe either a clockwise or counterclockwise circulation." (p. 53)
- **Twelve sovereign/waxing-waning hexagrams (bigua 辟卦 / xiaoxi gua 消息卦)**, Meng Xi (p. 78): Waxing: Fu 復 ䷗ (11th month) → Lin 臨 ䷒ (12th) → Tai 泰 ䷊ (1st) → Dazhuang 大壯 ䷡ (2nd) → Guai 夬 ䷪ (3rd) → Qian 乾 ䷀ (4th); Waning: Gou 姤 ䷫ (5th) → Dun 遯 ䷠ (6th) → Pi 否 ䷋ (7th) → Guan 觀 ䷓ (8th) → Bo 剝 ䷖ (9th) → Kun 坤 ䷁ (10th).
- **Jing Fang's Eight Palaces (bagong 八宮)** (pp. 81–82): each pure hexagram heads a palace; 5 "generations" (shi 世) formed "by changing one line of the pure hexagram to its opposite, starting at the bottom" (Qian → 1st gen Gou ䷫ (44), 2nd gen Dun ䷠ (33), etc.); then two more: "roaming soul" (you hun 游魂, 4th line of 5th generation changes) and "returning soul" (gui hun 歸魂, entire lower trigram changes back). 8 palaces × 8 = 64.
- **Lateral linkage (pangtong 旁通)**, Yu Fan: "all six lines of a hexagram change to their opposites" (p. 84) — the full-complement pairing operator.
- **Yilin (Forest of Changes)**, Jiao Yanshou: "each of the sixty-four hexagrams is paired with every other hexagram, plus itself, resulting in 64 x 64 = 4096 hexagram pairs... a codification of the result of using changing lines to derive a second hexagram" (pp. 79–80).

## 2. RULES (mechanical/formal)

### 2.1 Combinatorial closure
**R-A1.** 6 positions × 2 values = 64 hexagrams (p. 3).
**R-A2.** Changing lines map any hexagram onto any other: "depending on the numbers produced by the divination method, any hexagram can change into any other, yielding 64 × 64 = 4096 possible combinations. This includes the possibility that it can remain relatively static, with no changing lines." (p. 32)

### 2.2 Generation cosmogony (Xici A.11.5)
**R-A3.** "In change there is Supreme Polarity (taiji 太極), which generates the Two Modes. The Two Modes generate the Four Images, and the Four Images generate the Eight Trigrams." (p. 46) Taiji = "the cosmogonic state before the differentiation into yin and yang, yet already containing the principle of bipolarity." (pp. 46–47) Shao Yong's gloss: "One divides into two, two divides into four, and four divides into eight." (p. 99) Shao inserts two levels: "The Supreme Polarity is a unity. Without acting it generates duality; duality is spirit (shen 神). Spirit generates number; number generates images (xiang 象); images generate implements [concrete things]." (p. 98)

### 2.3 Three Powers → six lines
**R-A4.** Xici B.10.1: "It contains the Way of Heaven, it contains the Way of Humanity, and it contains the Way of Earth. It combines these Three Powers and doubles them, resulting in six [lines]." (p. 48)

### 2.4 Line-position grammar (Han xiangshu + Tuan zhuan concepts, pp. 39–40, 85)
**R-A5.** Correspondence (ying 應): "the corresponding lines in the two component trigrams (e.g., the first line in each) should have opposite yin/yang values... Thus the idea of correspondence is not matching or equivalence, but rather responding. The product is harmony, not sameness." (p. 39) — pairs: 1↔4, 2↔5, 3↔6.
**R-A6.** Centrality (zhong 中): positions 2 and 5 (p. 40).
**R-A7.** Correctness (zheng 正): yang in odd, yin in even positions (p. 40).
**R-A8.** Ruler: meaning-embodiment line or position 5 (p. 40).
**R-A9.** Waxing/waning (xiaoxi 消息) links natural cycles to behavior: "applies both to natural cycles and to the superior person (junzi), who adapts his behavior to the exigencies of the time." (p. 40)

### 2.5 Hexagram-transformation operators (Han xiangshu toolbox, pp. 78–85)
**R-A10.** Changing lines (divination) — see §2.6.
**R-A11.** "Hexagram fluctuation" (gua bian 卦變): "any method by which one hexagram changes into another, either through the application of changing lines in the divination process... or within a prescribed hexagram sequence, such as waxing and waning or the generations of the Eight Palaces." (p. 85)
**R-A12.** Eight Palaces generation rule (bottom-up single-line changes + roaming/returning soul rules) (pp. 81–82).
**R-A13.** Lateral linkage (pangtong): invert all six lines (p. 84).
**R-A14.** Interlocking trigrams: lines 2–4 and 3–5 (pp. 10, 81–82).
**R-A15.** Najia 納甲 "inserted stem": pure hexagrams ↔ heavenly stems: Qian=jia(1)+ren(9); Kun=yi(2)+gui(10); Gen=bing(3); Dui=ding(4); Kan=wu(5); Li=ji(6); Zhen=geng(7); Sun=xin(8) (Table 4.4, p. 83).
**R-A16.** Stems and branches (ganzhi 干支): 10 stems × 12 branches, "combined in pairs to count 1 through 60 — not 120... By this method one returns to the first stem and the first branch after 60" (p. 83); branches "also correlate with the directions, the seasons, the lunar months, the double-hours of the day, and the zodiacal animals." (p. 83)
**R-A17.** Guaqi 卦氣 "hexagram breaths" (Meng Xi): the 24 lines of the 4 cardinal "principal hexagrams" (Kan, Li, Zhen, Dui — "those that represent the four cardinal directions, based on the houtian or King Wen sequence of trigrams... when doubled") ↔ the 24 fifteen-day solar terms (pp. 78–79).

### 2.6 Divination — full algorithm (ch. 3, pp. 66–71)
**R-D1. Milfoil (yarrow) casting, Zhu Xi's reconstruction** of Xici A.9.3 ("The number of the Great Expansion is 50; those that are used are 49. Divide them in two, to symbolize the Two [Modes]. Place one [between the fingers] to symbolize the Three [Powers]. Count off by fours to symbolize the Four Seasons. Put the remainder between the fingers to represent the intercalary month...", p. 67):
1. Set aside 1 of 50 stalks.
2. Randomly divide remaining 49 into two bunches.
3. Take 1 from the right bunch, place between ring and little fingers of left hand.
4. Count off left bunch by fours; place remainder (≤4) between 3rd and 4th fingers.
5. Count off right bunch by fours; place remainder (≤4) between 2nd and 3rd fingers.
6. Stalks in left hand now = 9 or 5. Set aside → first "change" (bian 變).
7. Regather; repeat → left hand = 4 or 8 (second change); repeat again → 4 or 8 (third change).
8. Reduce: 9→8→2, 5→4→3 (i.e., 9 and 8 count as 2; 5 and 4 count as 3) [p. 69; Adler notes Zhu Xi "only poorly explains" this reduction].
9. Sum the three reduced values → 6, 7, 8, or 9 → line: 6 = changing yin (⚋x), 7 = unchanging yang, 8 = unchanging yin, 9 = changing yang (⚊x). Draw as bottom line.
10. Repeat 5 more times (bottom-up) to complete the hexagram.
11. If any changing lines: "draw another hexagram with those lines changed, yin to yang or yang to yin." (pp. 68–70)

**R-D2. Coin method** ("Fire Pearl Forest" huozhulin 火珠林, attributed to Jing Fang, first attested Tang, 7th c.): "One simply takes three coins, assigns the value 2 to one side and 3 to the other, and throws them together... yields either 6, 7, 8, or 9 for each line, so six throws yields a hexagram." (p. 71) Probability caveat: "the coin method does not produce the same probabilities as the milfoil method" (p. 71).

**R-D3. Zhu Xi's reading rules (Yixue qimeng) — which text answers the question** (pp. 70–71, verbatim):
- Qian with all six lines 9, or Kun with all six 6 → use the "Using all..." line text.
- 0 changing lines → original hexagram's Tuan statement; "taking the inner hexagram as zhen 貞 [the question, or present situation] and the outer hexagram as hui 悔 [the prognostication]."
- 1 changing line → that line's statement.
- 2 changing lines → both line statements, "but we take the upper line [of the two] as ruler."
- 3 changing lines → Tuan statements of both original and resulting hexagram; original = zhen, resulting = hui; "In the first ten hexagrams [of this sort] we make zhen the ruler; in the latter ten hexagrams we make hui the ruler."
- 4 changing lines → the two UNCHANGED lines of the RESULTING hexagram, "But we take the lower line as ruler."
- 5 changing lines → the one unchanged line of the resulting hexagram.
- 6 changing lines → Qian/Kun: both "Using all" texts; other hexagrams: Tuan of resulting hexagram.

**R-D4.** Interpretation posture: "the first hexagram can be understood as a representation or reading of the present situation and its direction of change, like a vector... the second hexagram would be not a predetermined future state but rather a representation of a possible future state to which the present situation is tending." (p. 32)
**R-D5.** Incipience (ji 幾): "Incipience is the subtle sign of activity, when the auspicious is first visible. The superior person sees incipience and acts, without waiting all day." (Xici B.5.11, p. 48) — the Yi "can detect the most minute signs of change before they express themselves" (p. 48).
**R-D6.** Oracle-bone precursor rule: binary "charge" questions ("The harvest will be good; the harvest will not be good"), repeated 5–10 times (p. 61); "there was no room for subtle interpretations... The responses were either favorable or unfavorable" (Keightley, quoted p. 75).

### 2.7 Hetu/Luoshu numerology
**R-H1.** Luoshu (Luo Text): numbers 1–9, "a 'magic square' of three, whose numbers in any direction add up to fifteen." (p. 89)
**R-H2.** Hetu (River Chart): numbers 1–10 as black/white dots; Xici A.9.1–2: "Heaven is 1, Earth is 2; Heaven is 3, Earth is 4; Heaven is 5, Earth is 6; Heaven is 7, Earth is 8; Heaven is 9, Earth is 10. The numbers of Heaven are five; the numbers of Earth are five... The numbers of Heaven [equal] 25 and the numbers of Earth [equal] 30. Together the numbers of Heaven and Earth are 55." (p. 89)
**R-H3.** Hetu phase-map (Figure 5.8a, p. 107): Bottom 1&6 Water; Top 2&7 Fire; Left 3&8 Wood; Right 4&9 Metal; Center 5&10 Earth.
**R-H4.** Luoshu trigram-map (Figure 5.8b, p. 107): 1 Kan/zi(1)/Water (bottom); 8 Gen/chou(2),yin(3)/Wood (lower left); 3 Zhen/mao(4)/Wood (left); 4 Sun/chen(5),si(6)/Metal (upper left); 9 Li/wu(7)/Metal (top); 2 Kun/wei(8),shen(9)/Fire (upper right); 7 Dui/you(10)/Fire (right); 6 Qian/xu(11),hai(12)/Water (lower right); 5 "Alone in the central palace."
**R-H5.** "The circle [Hetu] is the [movement of the] stars; the numbers of the calendrical record are founded on it. The square [Luoshu] is Earth; the method of drawing the Divisions and well-field plots is copied from it." (Shao Yong, p. 107)
**R-H6.** Shao Yong's cosmological chronology: "generations (shi 世, thirty years), revolutions (yun 運, twelve generations), epochs (hui 會, thirty revolutions), and cycles (yuan 元, twelve epochs). Doing the math, this makes one cycle equal to 129,600 years." (p. 98)

### 2.8 Five Phases cycles
**R-F1.** Mutual generation: "water generates wood... wood generates fire... fire generates earth (as ashes), earth generates metal (as ores), and metal generates 'water' or liquid (when melted)." (p. 23)
**R-F2.** Phases are not elements: "Elements are fundamental, indivisible building blocks... Phases, as the term suggests, are temporary stages in the continuous change and transformation of qi." (p. 23)

### 2.9 Xiantian/houtian epistemic rule
**R-X1.** "I understand xiantian to refer to analytic or mathematical/logical relationships, and houtian to empirical relationships... 'a priori' is the most accurate translation." (Adler, p. 106) "the Fuxi versions derive from the inherent logic of the figures." (p. 106) Shao Yong: "There was an Yi before [the hexagrams] were drawn." (p. 106)

---

## 3. SYNTAX / STRATA (textual layers)

### 3.1 The strata (oldest → latest)
1. **Hexagrams (gua)** — oldest layer, pre-1045 bce; possibly evolved from numbers (p. 29). Fuxi myth (pp. 6, 44–45: Xici A.4.2/B.4.2 "Looking up [Fuxi] contemplated the Heavenly patterns; looking down he examined the Earthly order... In this way he first created the Eight Trigrams, to spread the power/virtue (de 德) of his spiritual clarity and to classify the dispositions of the myriad things.").
2. **Hexagram names** — attributed to King Wen; "tags", weak connection to figures (p. 30).
3. **Hexagram statements / Judgments (guaci 卦辭 / tuan 彖)** — attributed to King Wen in prison (p. 6); "short, enigmatic statements of various types, including proverbs... and formulaic oracular pronouncements (such as 'auspicious,' 'danger,' 'misfortune,' 'disastrous')." (p. 32) Length: 2–29 characters, average ~9 (p. 33). Rutt: "Their importance in later practice derives neither from their content nor from their history... but simply from their position immediately after the hexagram. They are possibly the most defective section of Zhouyi." (p. 33)
4. **Line statements (yaoci 爻辭)** — attributed to the Duke of Zhou, "for each of the 384 hexagram lines" (p. 6); "the location of most of the oracular formulas in the text" (p. 35). Some hexagrams show internal coherence: hex 1 "dragon sequence" ("Hidden dragon... Flying dragon in Heaven... A dragon going too far", pp. 36–37) and hex 24 Fu (quoted p. 37).
5. **Basic text = Zhouyi**: layers 1–4, "strictly a divination manual" (p. 6), printed in two chapters (juan) divided 1–30 / 31–64 (p. 10).
6. **Ten Wings (Shiyi 十翼)** — "actually only seven of them (three are divided into two parts each that are counted separately)" (p. 8), dated 5th–2nd c. bce (p. 11):
   - 1–2. **Tuan zhuan 彖傳** (Commentary on the Judgments) — analyzes hexagram via component trigrams, firm/yielding, position, correspondence, centrality, correctness, ruler, xiaoxi (pp. 38–40).
   - 3–4. **Daxiang zhuan 大象傳** (Greater Images) + **Xiaoxiang zhuan 小象傳** (Smaller Images). Greater Image standard form: "[trigram imagery]: [hexagram name]. The superior person (junzi 君子) [maxim]." E.g. "Thunder and Wind: Everlasting. The superior person takes his stand and does not change direction." (p. 41) Smaller Images: brief glosses quoting the line texts (p. 42).
   - 5–6. **Xici zhuan 繫辭傳** (Appended Remarks / Great Treatise, Dazhuan) — "tantamount to a metaphysics of change — both ordered change (yin-yang alternation) and unordered change (the randomness at the heart of the divination process)." (p. 43)
   - 7. **Wenyan zhuan 文言傳** (Words of the Text) — only hexagrams 1–2; source of "Four Virtues" reading of yuan heng li zhen: "'Originating' (yuan) is the growth of goodness. 'Penetrating' (heng) is the gathering of excellence. 'Being appropriate' (li) is the harmonizing of rightness. 'Being correct' (zhen) is the basis of affairs." (p. 34)
   - 8. **Shuogua zhuan 說卦傳** (Discussing the Trigrams) — 22 passages; correlative imagery + the two/three trigram sequences (p. 52).
   - 9. **Xugua zhuan 序卦傳** (Sequence) — "probably a mnemonic device to help people remember the received sequence" (p. 56); rationale chains ("When things are produced they must be dim. Therefore what follows is Meng..." p. 57).
   - 10. **Zagua zhuan 雜卦傳** (Assorted Hexagrams) — antithetical pairs: "Qian [1, Creating] is firm, Kun [2, Complying] is yielding. Bi [8, Being Close] is happy; Shi [7, Army] is sad." (p. 57)

### 3.2 Formulaic phrases (the "grammar" of oracular pronouncements)
- "Beneficial [or not] to cross the great river" — 7 hexagram texts; "beneficial to see the great man" — 5 (p. 32).
- "yuan heng li zhen 元亨利貞" — entire Judgment of hexagram 1; "also occur as a group in five other hexagram statements, and one or more of them in fifty." (p. 34)
- Oracular outcome words: "auspicious," "danger," "misfortune," "disastrous"; "no blame" (wu jiu); "regret vanishes"; "Nothing is appropriate"; "ominous" — recurring in line texts (pp. 32, 35–36).
- 11 hexagram statements concern war/captives; many concern sacrifice (p. 33).

### 3.3 Interpretive syntax — two schools
- **Xiangshu 象數 (image and number)**: "focuses on the lines, trigrams, and hexagrams," their "developmental and transformational relations, their numerological values, and their symbolic correlations" (p. 76). Internal relations (positions, other lines, other hexagrams, component trigrams) vs. external/cosmological (pp. 78–79).
- **Yili 義理 (meaning and principle)**: "focuses on the hexagram texts, line texts, and appendices" (p. 76); Wang Bi: "When the name of the hexagram is mentioned, we have the ruling factor of all its concepts... contemplate the hexagram text, and the concept will be seen." (p. 93) Wang Bi's three-stage hermeneutic: words (yan) → images (xiang) → meaning (yi 意); "whoever retains only the words does not grasp the images, and whoever retains only the images does not grasp the meaning." (p. 93)
- Needham's verdict on xiangshu: "Its universal system of symbolism constituted a stupendous filing system." (p. 84)

### 4.8 Other diagram systems
- **Zhou Dunyi's Taiji Diagram (Taiji tu 太極圖)** (pp. 128–129): top circle (Supreme Polarity) → second level "interaction of yin and yang" with central small circle = Taiji → Five Phases level → yin/yang circles → "the myriad things."
- **Zhao Huiqian (1370s)**: "River Chart spontaneously [generated] by Heaven and Earth" — adds Eight Trigrams by name + black/white "seed" dots: "This is the earliest progenitor of the familiar yin-yang diagram seen frequently today." (p. 129)
- **Lai Zhide's Circular Diagram (Yuan tu 圓圖)** (pp. 129–130): empty center circle; legend: "What is complementary is number. What controls is principle (li). What flows is qi." Lai: "Therefore the diagram preceded Fuxi and King Wen." — "instead of number (shu) being the fundamental principle it is imagery (xiang)." (p. 130)
- **Table 7.1 — What the Yi does** (p. 155): Encompasses the Way; Natural: "discloses things"; Human: "completes efforts"; Inner: "penetrates purposes"; Outer: "resolves doubts," "determines undertakings."

## 6. KEY QUOTES (load-bearing, with pages)

- Definition: "Originally and at its core it is a manual of divination based on six-line diagrams called 'hexagrams,' dating back to the 11th or 12th century bce, with layers of text that were added between roughly the 9th and 3rd centuries bce." (p. 3)
- Process ontology: "what is fundamentally real is change, not permanence... it is a way of becoming, not being." (p. 20)
- The Yi as grammar: "The Yijing trigrams themselves eventually became part of the 'grammar' in which the natural world was described." (p. 19) And: "The kinds of associations described here provided the grammar for traditional Chinese correlative cosmology and the Chinese sciences." (p. 90) — direct warrant for the project's letters/syntax framing.
- Qi: "Qi covers the whole spectrum of mind and body, or matter and energy... Qi is also inherently dynamic, constantly changing and transforming in ordered ways. The Yijing is understood to be a device that can detect those changes so that people can adapt their behavior appropriately." (pp. 20–21)
- Bipolar closure: "reality is inherently bipolar; nothing can ever be solely yin or solely yang... a 'seed' of yin in yang and vice versa." (p. 22)
- Non-dualism: "neither yin nor yang is reducible to each other, but together they are complementary aspects of a more fundamental order (the dao) and are necessarily defined in relation to each other." (p. 28)
- Relational identity: "things (including people) are defined by their relationships with other things... those relationships are not secondary characteristics of a person's identity; they are definitional." (p. 25)
- Inductive divination = formal system: "Inductive divination involves a pre-established system of signs — a grammar or code which can be, and sometimes is, contained in a manual, like the Yijing." (p. 7)
- The oracle's address (Zhu Xi's invocation): "Prevailing upon you, supreme eternal milfoil... Only you have the spiritual power, so I beg that you clearly announce it." (p. 142)
- Yi as model: "the Yi is a model of Heaven and Earth. Therefore we can stitch together the threads of the Way of Heaven and Earth" (Xici A.4.1, quoted p. 73).
- Creativity without creator: "creation or creativity has no need of a transcendent source... Creativity is inherent in the natural world." (p. 126) Reversal: "what is ex nihilo is not the created substance but rather the dynamic reversal (fu 復) of the transformative process." (p. 126)
- Four uses: "The Yi contains the Way of the Sages in four respects: in speech we honor its phrases; in activity we honor its fluctuations; in making implements we honor its images; in divining we honor its prognostications." (Xici A.10.1, p. 46)
- Form boundary: "What is above form (xing'er shang 形而上) is called the Way; what is within form (xing'er xia 形而下) is called implements." (Xici A.12.4, p. 47)

## 7. MOST IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL FINDINGS
1. **A complete operator algebra is documented**: correspondence (ying, 1↔4/2↔5/3↔6 polarity-match), correctness (zheng), centrality (zhong), ruler; plus hexagram-to-hexagram operators: changing lines (4096 matrix), inversion (King Wen pairs), full complement (pangtong), nuclear extraction (2-4, 3-5), Eight Palaces bottom-up bit-flips (+roaming/returning soul), waxing-waning 12-cycle. The project can treat these as the formal transformation group on the 64-state space.
2. **The 6/7/8/9 layer is a pure/mixed parity detector**: maturity = numeric purity (2+2+2, 3+3+3) → the "old/new yin-yang" distinction is arithmetically grounded, and the divination algorithm (50→49→divide→count by 4s→remainders 9/5, 4/8→reduce to 2/3) is fully specified in both stalk and coin versions.
3. **Zhu Xi's 8-case reading rule** (§2.6 R-D3) is a complete deterministic decision table mapping number-of-changing-lines → which text stratum answers — effectively the "evaluation function" of the oracle automaton.
4. **Adler's xiantian = a priori / houtian = a posteriori** reading (p. 106) gives the project a clean Design-vs-Evolution split for the two arrangements, with "There was an Yi before [the hexagrams] were drawn" as the slogan of form preceding manifestation.
